Eﬃcient synthesis of tetrasubstituted 2,3-
allenoates and preliminary studies on bioactivities †
Yuan Yao,a Guirong Zhu,a Qin Chen,*a Hui Qian*a and Shengming Ma
 *a,b
A general and highly e ﬃcient straightforward protocol for the preparation of tetrasubstituted 2,3-alleno-
ates through a palladium-catalyzed coupling reaction of 3-alkoxycarbonyl propargylic carbonates and
boronic acids with commercially available tri( o-tolyl)phosphine as a ligand has been developed. This mild
reaction exhibited a wide substrate scope and functional group compatibility, providing a highly e ﬃcient
strategy to access valuable tetrasubstituted 2,3-allenoate products. Several tetrasubstituted 2,3-allenoates
obtained in this study exhibited potent anti-cancer and anti-diabetic activities.
Allenes are of great importance not only because of their
broad existence in natural products and biologically active
compounds as well as advanced materials but also due to their
versatility in organic synthesis as useful building blocks and
even ligands/catalysts.
1–5 2,3-Allenoates represent a particularly
useful subset of allenes with demonstrated reactivities, includ-
ing Morita –Baylis–Hillman reactions, 6 nucleophilic addition
reactions,7 electrophilic addition reactions, 8 rearrangements,9
and cyclization reactions. 10 In the past few decades, substan-
tial e ﬀorts have been devoted to the synthesis of 2,3-alleno-
ates.11 Wittig11a,b or Horner –Wadsworth–Emmons reaction, 11c
isomerization of alkynoates, 11d–f β-hydride elimination of ( E)-
enol triflates, 11g,h cross-coupling of α-diazoesters with alky-
nes,11i,j and caboxylation 11k–r are the common approaches.
However, limitations still remain for the synthesis of tetrasub-
stituted 2,3-allenoates: trapping of allenyl anions with electro-
philes (Scheme 1a) developed by Hammond, Maruoka, and
Feng et al. ,
12a–d the reaction of silyl alkynyl ketene acetals with
electrophiles reported by List et al. ,12e and phosphine-cata-
lyzed ring opening reactions of cyclopropenonyl acetates
observed by Shi et al. (Scheme 1b) may a ﬀord tetrasubstituted
2,3-allenoates.
12f Recently, our laboratory reported the syn-
thesis of tetrasubstituted 2,3-allenoates from readily available
tertiary 2-alkynols (Scheme 1c).
11p
During the past few decades, palladium-catalyzed coupling
of propargylic derivatives with organometallic reagents has
been used for the synthesis of allenes. 13 We envisioned to
develop an e ﬃcient CO-free synthesis of tetrasubstituted 2,3-
allenoates from readily available 3-alkoxycarbonyl-substituted
propargylic carbonates and commercially available boronic
acids via Suzuki coupling (Scheme 1d).
Scheme 1 Diﬀerent protocols for the synthesis of tetrasubstituted 2,3-
allenoates.

In our initial studies, 3-methoxycarbonyl-substituted pro-
pargylic carbonate 1a and phenylboronic acid 2a were used as
model substrates. When a mixture of 1a and 2a was treated
with the semi-labile bidentate o-(diphenylphosphino)benz-
aldehyde (L1),13w only 2% yield of the desired 2,3-allenoate 3aa
was observed. Zheda-Phos L2 14 did not give any allenoate
product. DPEPhos and rac-BINAP also failed in promoting the
reaction e ﬃciently. We were delighted to find that when the
simplest phosphine ligand PPh 3 was employed in the reaction
system, the desired product could be obtained smoothly with
53% yield. Interestingly, the commercially available ligand P( o-
tol)3
13x was more e ﬃcient, a ﬀording allenoate 3aa with 78%
yield (Table 1).
Other parameters were then investigated (Table 2). [Pd(allyl)
Cl]2 was much less e ﬃcient (entry 1). Although Pd 2(dba)3,
Pd(OAc)2, and Pd(PPh 3)4 could give the desired allenoate 3aa,
Pd2(dba)3·CHCl3 was still the most e ﬃcient (entries 2 –5).
Subsequently, di ﬀerent solvents were also surveyed. MeCN
failed to provide better results, toluene a ﬀorded 87% yield,
and the yield increased to 92% when THF was used (entries
6–8). We were pleased to find that the catalyst loading could be
reduced to 1 mol%, and water was not necessary for this trans-
formation even at 25 °C (entries 9 and 10) as compared to
what was reported in our previous study. 13x
With the established reaction conditions in hand, we next
examined the reaction scope. As shown in Table 3, a wide
range of 3-methoxycarbonyl-2-alkynylic carbonates 1 and
boronic acids 2 may form the desired tetrasubstituted 2,3-
allenoates 3 with excellent e ﬃciency and regioselectivity (no
alkyne products were observed in all cases). A variety of func-
tional groups, such as phenol ( 3ae), nitro ( 3af), ester ( 3ag),
aldehyde ( 3ah), and halides ( 3ai and 3cm) survived under the
standard conditions. The aryl boronic acids with the methoxy
group at di ﬀerent positions all reacted smoothly to give the
desired products 3bb–3bd, although the reaction was slower
when the methoxy group was at the ortho-position, probably
due to steric hindrance ( 3bd). 2-Naphthyl or 3-thienyl boronic
acid could also produce 2,3-allenoates 3ak and 3al with over
80% yields. It is worth mentioning that the bulky substituent
in propargylic carbonate would not a ﬀect the e ﬃciency ( 3cm).
Synthetically useful functional groups, such as acetal ( 3ea) and
the C vC bond ( 3fa) could be installed in the propargylic
carbonates.
This protocol can be conducted well on a gram-scale: reac-
tion of 1a and 1b aﬀorded 3aa and 3ba in 88% and 77% yield,
respectively (eqn (1) and (2)).

through bromolactonisation.15 Treatment with Et 2Zn a ﬀorded

A plausible mechanism is shown in Scheme 3: the allenyl-
palladium intermediate I generated from the S N2′-type oxi-
dative addition of a Pd(0) complex with the propargylic carbon-
ates underwent transmetalation with arylboronic acids to give
the allenylpalladium intermediate II, which resulted in the for-
mation of 2,3-allenoates via reductive elimination.
Finally, we were also intrigued by the potential biological
activities of these newly synthesized tetrasubstituted 2,3-
allenoates, and thus their cytotoxicity against A549 human
lung cancer cells was evaluated. Cell growth was measured by
the sulforhodamine B (SRB) assay. The inhibition e ﬀect of the
compounds on cell growth was firstly screened at 10 μM, and
then those with an inhibitory rate higher than 50% were
further investigated and IC

bility by 50%) were measured. As shown in Table 4,
Compounds 3ah, 3ai, 3ak, 3fa, 4, 5, and 7 displayed marginal
activity against the growth of A549 cells, whereas the rest of
the compounds exhibited significant cytotoxicity with IC
50si n
the low micromolar range. Among them, 3dn showed the most
potent activity with an IC 50 of 2.4 μM, suggesting that it might
be a promising anticancer agent for further investigation.
We also tested the potential activity of these tetrasubsti-
tuted 2,3-allenoates against diabetes. Glucagon-like peptide-1
(GLP-1) plays a critical role in limiting postprandial blood
glucose and thus becomes an important target for developing
new therapies for type II diabetes. STC-1 mouse intestinal
endocrine cells were treated with the tested compounds and
the extracellular level of GLP-1 was determined. As shown in
Table 5, 3aa, 3ag, 3aj, 3ak, 3dn, and 3fa eﬀectively stimulated
the secretion of GLP-1 at 100 μM, which was more than 90% of
that in the presence of the positive control PMA (1 μM).
Furthermore, these six compounds were tested at a range of
lower concentrations and the half maximal e ﬀective concen-
tration (EC
50) was measured. Notably, 3aa and 3dn were the
most potent with an EC 50 of ∼3 μM. Further investigations of
the potential antidiabetic activity and the mechanisms are
underway.
Conclusions
In summary, we have presented a straightforward protocol to
prepare tetrasubstituted 2,3-allenoates from a wide range of
3-alkoxycarbonyl propargylic carbonates and boronic acids via
palladium-catalysis under mild conditions with good to excel-
lent yields tolerating syntheticen useful functional groups.
These highly functionalized allenoate products may be easily
transformed to other useful molecules. Preliminary biological
studies found that several tetrasubstituted 2,3-allenoates
exhibited both anti-cancer and anti-diabetic activities. Further
studies including enantioselective synthesis of tetrasubstituted
2,3-allenoates via Suzuki-coupling are being conducted in our
laboratory.
